title: Tosefta Shabbat
text: [There are] four domains for purposes of the Sabbath. A private domain and a public domain*alt., "A private domain, a public domain, a carmelit (כרמלית), and an exempt domain (מקום פטור) (see GR"A): What is a private domain? A furrow that is ten [handbreadths] deep and four wide, and so too a fence that is ten high and four wide: that is a full-fledged private domain. What is a public domain? A highway and a large plaza, and alleyways that are open at both ends: that is a full-fledged public domain. They may not carry out from this private domain to that public domain, and they may not carry into this pubic domain from that private domain, and if one carried out or carried in unwittingly, he is liable for a sin-offering. Intentionally, he is punished with excision and is stoned. It is the same whether one carries out or carries in or extends [his hand holding an object] or throws [an object] -- he is liable.

But a sea and a valley and a carmelit and a colonnade and the threshold [of a door] are neither a private domain nor a public domain. They may not carry and place [an object] inside them, and if one carried and placed, he is exempt. They may not take out [an object] from inside them to a public domain, or from a public domain to inside them, and they may not bring [an object] from inside them to a private domain, or from a private domain to inside them, and if one took it out or brought it in, he is exempt. The courtyard of the masses and the alleyways that are not open on both ends: [If] they made an eruv [these actions] are permitted, [and if] they did not make an eruv, they are prohibited.

A man standing on the threshold may give [an object] to the homeowner, and the homeowner may give to him; he may give to a poor person [standing in the public domain] and the poor person may give to him; he may take from the homeowner and give to the poor person, [or take] from the poor person and give to the homeowner, and all three of them are exempt. Others say, a threshold services both domains. Whenever the entryway is open, it is like the inside [of the house], [and whenever] the entryway is shut, it is like the outside [of the house]. [If] its height was ten handbreadths and its width was four, behold, it is a domain in and of itself.

In the same way that they break off for the recitation of the Shema (see Shab. 1:2), so too they break off for the recitation of the Megillah, the recitation of Hallel, and the blowing of the shofar, and the shaking of the lulav, and every commandment stated in the Torah.

A tailor should not go out with his needle on Erev Shabbat*The phrase "Erev Shabbat" (Sabbath Eve) as used in the Mishnah and Tosefta generally refers to Friday afternoon before Shabbat commences. close to dusk, lest he forget and and go out [into the public domain]. Nor should a carpenter [go out] with the wood chip [used for measuring] that is around his neck, nor the dyer with his samples that are around his ear, nor the moneychanger with the dinar that is around his ear, nor the wool-comber with the cord [used for tying wool bundles] that is around his neck, but if they did go out, all of them are exempt, the words of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda says, a craftsman [who carries an object] in the typical manner of his craft is liable, and all other people are exempt. A peddler should not go out with the clothing [that he is selling] folded and laid upon his shoulders into the public domain, and if he did go out [in this way], behold, he is liable. A person should not go out with money wrapped in his kerchief into the public domain, and if he did go out, behold, he is liable.

They may go out with tefillin at dusk and read from Holy Scriptures at dusk, but they may not read at nighttime on Shabbat by the light of a lamp, even one taller than himself, and even [if the lamp is shining] in another house, and even [if there are] ten houses, this one inside of that one. But he may gaze [at the reflection of a lamp] inside a plate and he need not be concerned. Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel says, children may practice their parashot at nighttime on Erev Shabbat by the light of a lamp. Said Rabbi Yishmael, "One time I was reading by the light of a lamp, and I sought to tilt it (i.e., to better illuminate the page). I said, how great are the words of the Sages, who say, they may not read by the light of a lamp at nighttime on Shabbat." Rabbi Natan says, "He actually did tilt it, and he wrote in his notebook, 'Yishmael ben Elisha tilted the lamp on Shabbat. When the Holy Temple is rebuilt, he will bring a sin-offering.'"

Said Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, come and see to what extent ritual purity was widespread [in Israel*בישראל (MS Erfurt)], for the earlier [generations of Sages] did not institute a decree saying, "A pure man should not eat together with a menstruant," for the earlier ones would [certainly] not eat together with menstruants; rather, they [went further and] said, "A zav should not eat together with a zavah" (Shab. 1:3), in order not to accustom him to sin. Similarly, Beit Shammai say, "A zav who is a Pharisee should not eat together with a zav who is an am ha'aretz," but Beit Hillel allow it.*In the Bavli (Shab. 13a:2), the opinion of Beit Shammai is presented as that of the Sages.

These are among the halachot that were stated in the upper chamber of Chananiah ben Chizkiyahu ben Gurion when they went up to visit him. They took a vote, and Beit Shammai outnumbered Beit Hillel, and [the Sages] decreed eighteen matters on that very day. And that was as hard on them, on Israel, as the day on which the golden calf was made. Rabbi Eliezer says, that very day, they overfilled the measure [of laws]. Rabbi Yehoshua says, that very day, they abolished the measure, for whenever a measure is being filled, a person places [additional items] inside of it [in order to fill it], [and when it surpasses] the brim, he takes out that which is inside of it. That very day, they stated, "Any movable object conveys impurity if it is as thick as an ox goad" (Kel. 17:8), and they voted, and Beit Shammai outnumbered Beit Hillel. That very day, they stated, "One who forgets his vessels under a drainpipe on Erev Shabbat at dusk,"*Per Minchat Bikkurim and Minchat Yitzchak, this decree does not strictly refer to the Sabbath, but to any day of the week, and corresponds to the rule at Mishnah Mikvaot 4:1 that a vessel left under a drainpipe renders the water "drawn water," which invalidates a mikveh (see Shab. 16b:7) and they voted, and Beit Shammai outnumbered Beit Hillel.

Said Beit Shammai to Beit Hillel, "Do you not concede that meat and eggs may not be roasted on Erev Shabbat at dusk unless there is enough [time] for them to be [completely] roasted [by nightfall]? [Thus,] even ink, herbs, and vetch, and the like [must be fully soaked in water before nightfall (see Shab. 1:5)]." Beit Hillel said to them, "Do you not concede that beams may be laid down in an olive press and rollers suspended in a wine press on Erev Shabbat at dusk? [Thus,] even ink, herbs, and vetch, and the like." These stood behind their response and those stood behind their response, except that Beit Shammai say (Ex. 20:9), "Six days you shall labor and do all your work" -- that all your work be completed from [before] Erev Shabbat. And Beit Hillel say (Ex. 23:12), "Six days shall you do your work" -- that you shall do it all six days (but once a process has begun, it may continue on its own during the Sabbath).

Beit Shammai say, [Jews] may not [stop to] sell to a Gentile, nor load [an animal] with him, nor lift [a burden] onto him (i.e., his shoulders), unless there is enough [time] for him to arrive to a near place [before Shabbat], but Beit Hillel permits it. What is a "near place"? Until he arrives at a house adjacent to the [city] wall.*Alt., "Until he arrives at his own house, the words of Beit Shammai. And Beit Hillel say, until he arrives at a house adjacent to the [city] wall." (Minchat Yitzchak.) Rabbi Akiva says, enough time for him to go out from the entrance [of his house] and sanctify the day upon it. Said Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Tzadok, those of the house of Rabban Gamaliel would carry white garments to a Gentile launderer three days before Shabbat, and colored [garments even] on Erev Shabbat. And incidentally we learned that white [garments] are more difficult to launder than colored ones.

They may conduct water [via a canal] into a garden on Erev Shabbat at dusk, and it may be continuously watered on Shabbat. They may place a compress on the eye and a plaster on a wound on Erev Shabbat at dusk, and these may continuously provide healing on Shabbat. They may place sulfur under [silver] vessels on Erev Shabbat [in order to color them], and they may be continuously sulfured on Shabbat. They may place incense on top of coals on Erev Shabbat at dusk, but they may only place wheat kernels in a water mill if there is enough [time] for them to be ground [before Shabbat].

...Rabbi Tarfon says, one may light only with olive oil. Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri stood on his feet, and said: And what shall the people of Babylonia, who have only sesame oil, do? And what shall the people of Medea, who have only nut oil, do? And what shall the people of Alexandria, who have only radish oil, do? And what shall the people of Cappadocia, who have neither this nor that but only naphtha, do?...
17 One who takes out [to the public domain] a domesticated animal, a wild animal or fowl, whether live or dead is liable. R. Natan says: For dead ones he is liable, for live ones he is exempt.

They do not nurse from clean animals on holidays [and one needn't mention on shabbat. Abba Shaul says: they used to nurse from clean animals on a holiday.] A woman should not release milk from her breasts or express milk into a cup or dish in order to nurse her child. They do not nurse from either a gentile or an unclean animal, but if it is a matter of danger (to life), it is permitted, in that there is nothing that should stand before saving a life except for idol worship, forbidden sexual relationships, and shedding blood.

One may not lift an animal, a wild animal, or a bird from a private domain—needless to say from a public domain. However, one may push them until they enter. One may place a basket in front of the chicks so that they may climb up and climb down on it, but it is forbidden to move the basket.

One who reacts swiftly to a danger to a human life on the Sabbath, and one who is vigilant, behold he is praiseworthy, and one need not obtain permission from the Beit Din. How so? One fell into the sea and he is unable to lift himself up, [or] his ship sank at sea and he is unable to lift himself up -- they may descend and lift him up from there, and there is no need to obtain permission from the Beit Din. [If] one fell into a pit and cannot raise himself out, they may dig out a segment [of earth from the pit, presumably to widen it] and descend and lift him out of there, and there is no need to obtain permission from the Beit Din. An infant that entered a house and cannot get out -- they may break down the doors of the house, even if they were made of stone, and take him out of there, and there is no need to obtain permission from the Beit Din. They may extinguish or place a barrier before a fire on the Sabbath, and one who is vigilant [in doing so], behold, he is praiseworthy, and there is no need to obtain permission from the Beit Din.

One who was bitten by a snake [on the Sabbath] -- they call a doctor for him [to come] from one place to another place, and they slaughter a chicken for him, and they harvest leeks for him to eat, and there is no need to tithe, the words of Rebbi. And Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel says, one does need to tithe.

They may heat water for a sick person on the Sabbath, whether for his peace of mind or for medical purposes, and they should not say, "Let us delay [heating it] for him lest he live." Rather, the uncertainty [of his survival] overrides the Sabbath, and not just the uncertainty on this Sabbath, but rather the uncertainty on [even] another Sabbath. And they should not say, "Let Gentiles or minors do these things"; rather, [they should be done] with adults among the Jewish people. They should not say, "These things should be done [in reliance] upon the word of a woman or upon the word a Gentile"; rather, their words combine together with the consent of a [male] Jew.

R. Yose said: Whence do we know that saving a life takes precedence over the Sabbath? As it is written. “…you shall observe my Sabbaths.” Is it possible that circumcision and the temple service and saving a life [do not take precedence over the Sabbath]? The Torah teaches “But” - a portion. There are times when you observe the Sabbath and times when you do not observe the Sabbath.  R. Elazar says: Circumcision takes precedence over the Sabbath because one is punished for it by karet (excision) after time. And the matter is a kal va’homer. If for one limb of him the Sabbath can be superseded, it is logical that the Sabbath should be superseded for all of him. They said to him: according to your reasoning just as in that case it is certain and not uncertain, so too here it must be certain and not uncertain.  R. Akiva said: And with respect to which was the Torah more stringent? With the temple service or with the Sabbath? [The Torah was more stringent] with the temple service than with the Sabbath, for the temple service takes precedence over the Sabbath and the Sabbath does not take precedence over the temple service. And the matter is a kal va’homer - if the temple service takes precedence over the Sabbath and a risk to life takes precedence over it, with regard to the Sabbath, which the temple takes precedence over - is it not logical that a risk to human life should supersede it? Behold, you have learned that a risk to life takes precedence over the Sabbath.

R. Aha said in the name of R. Akiva. Behold, it says: “If a thief is found tunneling in…” Is the house’s owner certain or uncertain? You must say he is uncertain. If they kill a person to save a life in a case of uncertainty, it is logical that they should push off the Sabbath, in order to save a life in a case of uncertainty.  Behold, the commandments were only given to Israel that they might live by them, as it is written “Which a man shall perform and live by them” - he shall live by them, and not die by them.  Nothing takes precedence over saving a life, save idolatry, sexual sins, and murder. In which circumstances are these things said? When it is not a time of persecution. But, when it is a time of persecution, even when it comes to the smallest of small commandments, a person should die for it, as it is written: “Do not profane my holy name” (Leviticus 22) and “the Lord made everything for his own sake” (Proverbs 16).

One may tear the covering that is on a [barrel] of wine or muryas [on Shabbos], as long as he does not intend to pour [from it]. One may not open sealed jugs [on Shabbos]; R' Shimon ben Gamliel permits [it].
One who bundles seeds to protect them from birds or melons to protect them from animals may bundle normally on shabbat as long as s/he does not clap, dance, or slap [thighs] as is done on a week day.
